pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 🌐 **Strand 3 — Communication Networks**
Sub-strand 3: Information Security

Data can be blocked, stolen, changed or faked as it travels across networks. In this unit you will learn the four major data threats and match each one with the protection methods that defend against it.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B8.3.3.1** Recognise data threats and security protections.

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B8.3.3.1.1** Describe the nature of four major data threats (interruption, interception, modification, fabrication).
- **B8.3.3.1.2** Map the protection methods to each of the four data threats (authorisation, authentication, encryption and decryption).

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 10.1 The Four Major Data Threats
- 10.2 Mapping Protection Methods to the Threats

**Core competencies developed:** Communication and Collaboration (CC8.2, CC9.1), Digital Literacy (DL6.5), Critical Thinking (CP5.5).

pages.title: The Four Major Data Threats
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.3.3.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- discuss threats that prevent information reaching its destination;
- discuss threats that cause data corruption;
- describe the nature of the four major data threats.
[[fig:c8-f15|Figure 14: The four major threats to data in transit]]
| **Threat** | **Nature** | **Principle attacked** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interruption | Data or a system is **destroyed, blocked or made unavailable**, so information cannot reach its destination | Availability | Cutting a cable; **Denial of Service (DoS)** attacks flooding a website; deleting files; ransomware; power failure; theft of a server |
| Interception | An unauthorised party **gains access** to data (reads or copies it) while it is stored or travelling | Confidentiality | Eavesdropping on Wi-Fi; wiretapping; spyware; shoulder-surfing a PIN; illegal copying of files |
| Modification | An unauthorised party **intercepts and changes** data before it reaches its destination, corrupting it | Integrity | Changing an account number in a payment instruction; altering exam scores; viruses corrupting files; man-in-the-middle attacks |
| Fabrication | An unauthorised party **creates fake data** and inserts it into the system, pretending to be a genuine sender | Authenticity (integrity) | Fake emails or SMS that appear to come from a bank (phishing/spoofing); fake transactions; adding false records to a database |

pages.title: The Four Major Data Threats (continued)
pages.body:
> 🧪 **Activity**
Watch a video on threats to data security. Then classify these events: (a) a hacker floods the WAEC results portal with traffic; (b) someone reads your SMS messages through spyware; (c) a fake SMS “from MTN MoMo” asks you to reverse a transaction; (d) a virus alters numbers in a spreadsheet. (a – interruption, b – interception, c – fabrication, d – modification)

pages.title: Mapping Protection Methods to the Threats
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.3.3.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explain authorisation, authentication, encryption and decryption;
- match protection methods to each threat.
| **Protection method** | **Meaning** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|
| Authentication | Proving **who you are** before access is given | Passwords, PINs, fingerprints/face ID (biometrics), one-time passwords (OTP), **two-factor authentication (2FA)**, digital certificates |
| Authorisation | Deciding **what an authenticated user is allowed to do** | User account levels (admin/standard), file permissions (read-only), access-control lists, role-based access |
| Encryption | Converting readable data (**plaintext**) into unreadable code (**ciphertext**) using a **key** | HTTPS (padlock), WhatsApp end-to-end encryption, BitLocker drive encryption, encrypted Wi-Fi (WPA2/WPA3) |
| Decryption | Converting ciphertext back to plaintext with the correct key, so only the intended receiver can read it | Your browser decrypting a bank web page |
[[fig:c8-f16|Figure 15: Encryption and decryption]]

pages.title: Mapping threats to protections
pages.body:
## Mapping threats to protections
| **Threat** | **Main protection methods** | **Other supporting measures** |
|---|---|---|
| Interruption | **Authentication** and **authorisation** stop unauthorised people from deleting data or shutting systems down | Backups, redundant servers, UPS and generators, firewalls, DoS protection, antivirus, physical security |
| Interception | **Encryption/decryption** makes intercepted data unreadable; **authentication** and **authorisation** control who can read it | Secure (HTTPS) websites, VPNs, avoiding public Wi-Fi for banking, privacy screens |
| Modification | **Authorisation** (read-only rights) prevents unauthorised changes; **encryption** and digital signatures/hashes reveal tampering | Audit logs, version history, antivirus |
| Fabrication | **Authentication** verifies the true sender (digital signatures, 2FA, verified sender IDs) | User awareness: verify messages through official channels; spam filters |
> 🎯 **BECE focus** Remember the pairs: **Interruption → Availability**, **Interception → Confidentiality**, **Modification → Integrity**, **Fabrication → Authenticity**.

pages.body:
> ✏️ **Review exercises** — answer these in your exercise book or on the computer, then check with your teacher.
## Short answer questions
1. Describe the four major data threats with an example of each.
2. Distinguish between authentication and authorisation.
3. Explain how encryption protects against interception.
4. Map each of the four threats to at least one protection method.
